analysis.one_liner: Makes the President reimburse taxpayers for security costs on trips to his own businesses and bars him from running companies in office.
analysis.headline: Introduced December 17, 2025 with 4 Democratic cosponsors and referred to three House committees; no hearing, vote, or further action has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require the President (and anyone the Secret Service protects under the same provisions, such as the Vice President) to pay the Treasury back for the cost of Secret Service protection and other government expenses whenever they travel in connection with a business the President owns or profits from. It would bar a sitting President from creating or operating a business, tax any income from such activity at 100 percent, prohibit soliciting donations for a presidential library while in office, and require quarterly reports from the President's immediate family certifying their business conduct does not enrich him. It would also remove the President and Vice President's access to a specific federal law for suing the government over injuries.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who currently cover the cost of Secret Service protection and other government expenses whenever the President or his protected family members travel to promote his own business properties, without reimbursement. The bill would shift those costs to the business activity itself and impose transparency rules on the family's business dealings and presidential library fundraising.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers who fund presidential travel protection

how_it_helps.text: Requires reimbursement to the Treasury for Secret Service protection and other government costs whenever a protectee travels domestically or abroad to further the business interests of an entity the President owns, controls, or profits from [S2].
Prohibits the President from creating, operating, or serving on the board of any business while in office, and imposes a 100 percent tax on any income earned from such activity [S2].

Requires immediate family members who engage in business conduct the President himself is barred from to file quarterly reports to Congress and certify publicly that their conduct is not enriching the sitting President [S2].

Bans the President from soliciting donations for a presidential library or museum while in office, and requires annual financial reporting to the Archivist from the President and from private entities administering or lobbying for a presidential library, with a $1,000-a-day fine for late reports [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The President's own business interests and immediate family, who would bear the travel security reimbursement, the business-activity tax, and new reporting obligations; presidential library fundraising entities would face new reporting duties.
analysis.who_pays_short: The President's businesses and family holdings

drawbacks.text: The enforcement design leans on self-reporting: family members would certify their own compliance, and the Archivist's reports depend on the private entities filing accurately, so accountability depends on honest paperwork rather than independent audits [S2].

The bill's restrictions on a sitting President's business activities and the 100 percent tax raise structural questions about Congress's authority over the President's personal affairs that would likely be tested in court, and drawing the line between personal travel and business travel for Secret Service purposes could be contentious [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — taxpayers should not pay to protect a President on trips that promote his own businesses — has a clear, direct benefit and a modest administrative cost. The weaknesses are in execution: self-certification and after-the-fact reports are a weak check, and some provisions (like the 100 percent tax on business income and the tort-claims change) are broad enough to invite constitutional challenges. On balance, the taxpayer protections are real, but the enforcement teeth are soft.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on December 17, 2025 and sent to three House committees — Oversight, Judiciary, and Ways and Means — where it has sat with no hearing or vote [S4].

narrative.text: Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman introduced the bill with Reps. McIver and Tlaib on December 17, 2025 [S2].
The Speaker referred it to the Oversight and Government Reform, Judiciary, and Ways and Means committees, splitting it across three panels at once [S4].
It has four cosponsors, all Democrats, and no further action has been recorded since introduction [S3] [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the status quo holds: the sitting President's businesses continue to benefit from unreimbursed government costs on business-related travel, since the bill has not moved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The President's business interests, for now

for.name: Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman
for.role: Sponsor, House member from New Jersey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its lead sponsor.

for.name: Reps. LaMonica McIver and Rashida Tlaib
for.role: Original cosponsors, House members from New Jersey and Michigan
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all four cosponsors are Democrats; no Republicans have signed on, and with Republicans holding the House majority, the bill's committee referrals have so far produced no hearings or votes [S3] [S4].

industries.industry: Presidential family business holdings (e.g., the Trump Organization)
industries.note: The bill's reimbursement requirement, business-operations ban, 100 percent income tax, and family reporting rules all target the financial benefit the President's companies get from government-funded protection and travel while he is in office. Their gain today comes directly from costs the public bears.

industries.industry: Presidential library foundations and fundraising entities
industries.note: These private entities would face a ban on presidential donation solicitation and new annual financial reporting to the Archivist, aimed at limiting large gifts from interested parties while a president is in office.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors, a split referral across three committees, and no action in the weeks since introduction, the bill is very unlikely to receive a committee hearing or a floor vote in this Congress.
